summary: Specifies the IPv6 Flow Label field and the minimum requirements for nodes that label flows, forward labeled packets, and set up flow state. The label lets devices classify flows using only fixed-position fields in the main header. It replaces RFC 3697 and updates RFC 2205 and RFC 2460.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 packets carry a 20-bit Flow Label in their header. A sender puts the same value on all the packets of one flow, and a router can then treat that flow on its own without reading the rest of the packet. The field is simple, but it is not protected, so routers are told not to rely on it alone.

subtitle: A 20-bit field in the IPv6 header that lets routers tell flows apart without reading the packet's payload.

tldr.problem: Routers that classify traffic usually need the source address, destination address, ports and protocol, and those fields may be missing behind extension headers, fragmentation or encryption. Classifying on them is slow and awkward.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv6 header carries a 20-bit Flow Label. A source node gives every flow the same label, and routers identify the flow from the label together with the source and destination addresses, using only fields in fixed positions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC replaces RFC 3697 and updates RFC 2205 and RFC 2460. It also warns that the label is unprotected, so routers must not depend on it alone when spreading load across links.

sections.title: What the Flow Label Is For
sections.content:
From the viewpoint of the network layer, a flow is a sequence of packets sent from a particular source to a particular unicast, anycast or multicast destination that a node desires to label as a flow. From an upper-layer viewpoint, a flow could consist of all packets in one direction of a specific transport connection or media stream, but a flow is not necessarily mapped one to one to a transport connection.

Traditionally, flow classifiers have been based on the 5-tuple of source address, destination address, source port, destination port and transport protocol type. Some of these fields may be unavailable because of fragmentation or encryption, or because locating them past a chain of IPv6 extension headers is inefficient. Classifiers that depend only on IP-layer headers also make it easier to add new transport-layer protocols later. Using the 3-tuple of the Flow Label, Source Address and Destination Address instead enables efficient flow classification that uses only IPv6 main header fields in fixed positions.

The flow label can be used in both stateless and stateful scenarios. A stateless scenario is one where no node that processes the label needs to store information about a flow before or after a packet is processed. A stateful scenario is one where such a node stores information about the flow, and may need a signaling mechanism to tell downstream nodes how the label is being used. RSVP and GIST can signal flow label values. The minimum level of IPv6 flow support consists of labeling the flows, and a specific goal is to encourage the use of the label for stateless load distribution across Equal Cost Multi-Path and Link Aggregation Group paths. IPv6 source nodes SHOULD be able to label known flows, such as TCP connections and application streams, even when the node itself does not need any flow-specific treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is a run of packets that a node wants to treat together. The label lets a router do that by looking at fixed positions in the IPv6 header, which avoids hunting through extension headers or working around encryption.

sections.title: The Field and the Three-Part Flow Identifier
sections.content:
The 20-bit Flow Label field in the IPv6 header is used by a node to label packets of a flow. A Flow Label of zero indicates packets that have not been labeled. Packet classifiers can use the triplet of Flow Label, Source Address and Destination Address fields to identify the flow to which a particular packet belongs. Packets are then processed in a flow-specific manner by nodes that can do so statelessly or that have been set up with flow-specific state.

Flow label values should be chosen so that their bits show a high degree of variability, which makes them suitable as input to a hash function used in a load distribution scheme. At the same time, third parties should be unlikely to guess the next value a source of flow labels will choose. In statistics, a discrete uniform distribution is one in which each value in a range of equally spaced values is equally likely to be chosen next, and such a distribution shows both variability and unguessability, so an approximation to it is preferable as the source of flow label values. Intentionally, the RFC places no precise mathematical requirements on the distribution or on the method used to achieve it.

Once set to a non-zero value, the Flow Label is expected to be delivered unchanged to the destination node or nodes. A forwarding node MUST either leave a non-zero flow label value unchanged or change it only for compelling operational security reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is 20 bits wide, and zero means the packet is not labeled. A flow is identified by the label plus the two addresses. Routers pass a non-zero label through unchanged, and the label values should look random so they spread load evenly and cannot be guessed.

sections.title: Setting the Label in the Stateless Case
sections.content:
To enable Flow-Label-based classification, source nodes SHOULD assign each unrelated transport connection and application data stream to a new flow. A typical definition of a flow for this purpose is any set of packets carrying the same 5-tuple of destination address, source address, protocol, destination port and source port. A source node always has convenient and efficient access to this 5-tuple, which is not always the case for nodes that later forward the packet.

It is RECOMMENDED that source hosts set the flow label field for all packets of a given flow to the same value, chosen from an approximation to a discrete uniform distribution. The algorithm SHOULD ensure that the resulting values are unique with high probability. If two simultaneous flows are assigned the same value by chance and have the same source and destination addresses, they simply receive the same flow label treatment throughout the network, which as a low-probability event will not significantly affect load distribution. A possible stateless algorithm is a suitable 20-bit hash of values from the packet's 5-tuple, and Appendix A of the RFC gives an example. An alternative is a pseudo-random number generator per transport session, which requires the source node to keep the label associated with each transport socket. An implementation in which flow labels are assigned sequentially is NOT RECOMMENDED, as it would be simple for on-path observers to guess the next value. A source node that does not otherwise set the flow label MUST set its value to zero.

A node that forwards a flow whose arriving packets carry a zero label MAY change the label, and in that case it is RECOMMENDED that it set a uniformly distributed value as described for source nodes. The complete 5-tuple may not be available to a forwarding node, in particular for fragmented packets, so a flow can be defined by fewer IPv6 header fields, typically the 2-tuple of destination address and source address. A forwarding node might use the 5-tuple when possible and the 2-tuple otherwise, or the 2-tuple in all cases. Setting the label in a forwarding node would presumably be of value in first-hop or ingress routers, but it places a considerable per-packet processing load on them, so it MUST be a configurable option, disabled by default.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender should give every flow one label and keep it the same for all its packets, picking the value so it looks random. Numbering labels one after another is discouraged, because an observer could guess the next one. A sender that does not use labels must set the field to zero.

sections.title: Flow State Establishment
sections.content:
A node that sets the flow label MAY also take part in a flow state establishment method that results in assigning specific treatments to specific flows, possibly including signaling. Any such method MUST NOT disturb nodes taking part in the stateless scenario. A node that sets flow label values according to a stateful scheme MUST therefore choose labels that conform to the stateless rules in the previous section.

The RFC places the details of stateful models, signaling, specific flow state establishment methods and their related service models out of scope. Its basic requirement for stateful models is the one stated in this section: a stateful scheme must not break the stateless case, and its labels must look the same as labels chosen under the stateless rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A network may use the label to give some flows special treatment, but only if it does so without disturbing ordinary label use. Any label used that way must still follow the same rules as a plain stateless label.

sections.title: A Correction to RFC 2205 and What Changed
sections.content:
RFC 2460 reduced the size of the flow label field from 24 to 20 bits, and the references to a 24-bit flow label field in Section A.9 of RFC 2205 are updated accordingly. That is the essential correction this RFC carries.

The RFC lists the main differences between itself and its predecessor RFC 3697. It encourages non-zero flow label values to be used and clearly defines how to set a non-zero value. It encourages a stateless model with uniformly distributed flow label values. It does not specify any details of a stateful model. It retains the rule that the flow label must not be changed en route, but allows routers to set the label on behalf of hosts that do not do so. And it discusses the covert channel risk and its consequences for firewalls. The RFC also replaces Section 6 and Appendix A of RFC 2460, and points to RFC 6436 for the rationale behind the changes.
sections.plainLanguage: This document replaces RFC 3697. It fixes a stale reference in RFC 2205 that still described the label as 24 bits wide, and it adds guidance on choosing label values and on the risk of using the label as a covert channel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The flow label is not protected in any way, even when IPsec authentication is in use, so it can be forged by an on-path attacker. Implementers are advised that any en-route change to the flow label value is undetectable. On the other hand, a uniformly distributed pseudo-random flow label cannot be readily guessed. If a hash algorithm is used, it SHOULD include a step that makes the value significantly difficult to predict even with knowledge of the algorithm being used.

The label could be used as a covert data channel, because apparently pseudo-random values could in fact carry hidden data, for example in a series of otherwise innocuous UDP packets or in the labels of successive packets of a TCP session. Where the risk is significant, the only certain defense is for a firewall to rewrite non-zero flow labels, which is an exceptional violation of the rule that a non-zero label must not be changed; such a firewall SHOULD rewrite labels the way a forwarding node would, as if the incoming value were zero, and MUST NOT set non-zero labels to zero.

Because flow-specific treatment is triggered by the addresses and the label, an adversary may obtain a class of service the network did not intend to provide by modifying the IPv6 header or injecting packets with false addresses or labels, and a denial-of-service attack becomes possible when modified or injected traffic depletes the resources available to forward it and other traffic. An attacker could set all flow labels reaching a router to the same arbitrary non-zero value, or cycle the values quickly so that the packets of one flow each carry a different value. Stateless classifiers should therefore not use the flow label alone to control load distribution, and stateful classifiers should include explicit methods to detect and ignore suspect values.

IPsec does not include the Flow Label in any of its cryptographic calculations, so changing the label cannot fail an IPsec integrity check, and IPsec provides no defense against a man-in-the-middle changing it. IPsec tunnel mode protects the inner header's flow label, and the inner header's label must not be changed during decapsulation. The Flow Label also does nothing to remove the need for packet filtering based on headers past the IP header.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing protects the label, so an attacker on the path can change it or forge it, and nobody can tell afterwards. A firewall can rewrite labels to stop hidden data being carried in them, but that breaks the promise that a label stays unchanged. Routers must also mix the label with other fields when spreading load, so a forged label cannot hijack traffic.

viz.caption: THE EXAMPLE 20-BIT HASH FROM APPENDIX A, REFORMATTED AS STEPS

data.title: Example 20-bit hash function
data.code:
1. Split the destination and source addresses into two 64-bit values each, transforming the 5-tuple into a 7-tuple.
2. Add the five components together using unsigned 64-bit arithmetic, discarding any carry bits: both parts of the source address, both parts of the destination address, and the protocol number.
3. Apply the von Neumann algorithm to the resulting 64 bits: starting at the least significant end, select two bits; discard them if they are 00 or 11; output 0 for 01 and 1 for 10; stop when 16 bits have been output or the 64-bit string is exhausted.
4. Add the two port numbers to the resulting 16-bit number.
5. Shift the resulting value 4 bits left, and mask with 0xfffff.
6. In the highly unlikely event that the result is exactly zero, set the flow label to 1.
